name: Green fragrances

lead: Green fragrances are scents dominated by the smell of leaves, stems and cut grass. In perfumery they sit in the fresh family, where galbanum is the usual example of a green note.

People wear them to project a clean, crisp impression as part of grooming, a sensory counterpart to a fresh haircut or clear skin. Pairing a scent with the setting, such as daytime or warm weather, is how the style is typically used.

paras: Wearers choose a green-leaning cologne or eau de toilette and apply it as part of a normal grooming routine, often for daytime and warmer seasons. Fragrance communities describe green scents with terms such as leafy, herbal and grassy.
Fragrance ingredients can cause skin irritation or allergic reactions in some people. Fragrance preference is personal, and strong scents may not suit every setting.

chain: Smell crisp and fresh to others
angle.text: Wearers use green scents to complete a clean, fresh grooming impression. The effect is on how a person is perceived by smell rather than on their physical features.

lead: Green fragrances are perfumes whose main character comes from fresh-cut grass, leaves and stems. In Michael Edwards' fragrance wheel, Green is one of four subfamilies of the Fresh family, alongside Aromatic, Citrus and Water, and galbanum is its example green note.[1]

The style is usually traced to Vent Vert, created by perfumer Germaine Cellier for Balmain in 1947. Wikipedia's biography of Cellier says it used a high dose of galbanum, about 8 percent, and describes it as considered the first green perfume.[2]
People use green fragrance as a styling choice: it is chosen for a crisp, natural, clean impression as part of overall grooming. The appearance link is presentation rather than physical change.

paras: Fragrance families are rough groupings that overlap across sources.[1] Green notes evoke freshly cut grass, leaves and plant stems, and galbanum, a resin, is the example cited for the Green subfamily.[1]

Germaine Cellier (1909-1976), a French perfumer trained as a chemist who worked at Roure Bertrand, created Bandit in 1944, Vent Vert in 1947 and Fracas in 1948.[2] Vent Vert, made for Balmain, used about 8 percent galbanum and is described as the first green perfume.[2]

Green fragrances are one of several scent directions that people pick to suit the season, setting and personal style. They are discussed in fragrance communities alongside citrus, aromatic and woody styles.
